title: Conditional breakpoints and watches
summary: Stop only when something is wrong, and watch a comparison.

say.never: A breakpoint in a loop that runs 500 times stops 500 times. A **conditional breakpoint** stops only when a condition you type is true. **Right-click** the red dot, choose **Edit Breakpoint**, type a condition, and press **Enter**. The dot gets a little **=** in it.
say.bit: Right-click the dot, **Edit Breakpoint**, type a condition: it stops only when that's true.

marks.label: stops only on a hot day

say.never: The **Watch** section (under Variables) shows anything you type, even a whole expression. Click **+**, type something like `a == b`, and press **Enter**. It updates every time the program pauses.
say.bit: Add expressions to **Watch** with +; they update at every pause.

board.code:
WATCH
  first == second: false
  first.equals(second): true

say.never: For `String`s, `==` asks "is this the **same object** in memory?" `.equals` asks "do they **say the same thing**?" Two strings can say exactly the same thing and still be different objects, especially strings built while the program runs. To compare what strings say, always use `.equals`.
say.bit: `==` on strings asks "same object?"; `.equals` asks "same text?". Use `.equals`.

steps.title: In your lesson: Stop only when it matters

say.never: In `Battery.lowestVolts`, put a breakpoint inside the loop and give it the condition `millivolts[i] < 0`. Debug `Main`. It stops once, on the bad reading. Read `i` in Variables: that's the number for `Answers.MISSING_SAMPLE_INDEX`. Then make the loop skip readings below 0. Think about what happens if the *first* reading is the bad one.
say.bit: Condition `millivolts[i] < 0`, read `i`, write it in Answers, then skip negatives (even the first one).

say.bit: **Watch** is under Variables: hover its title, click **+**, type an expression.
